https://www.dw.com/en/australia-jetstar-.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5IVbh Flights at the Sydney Airport were experiencing delays following the incident Image: Izhar Khan/REUTERS Advertisement Two passenger aircraft — a Jetstar and a Qatar Airways plane — came close to crashing into each other on the tarmac at Australia's busiest Sydney Airport on Sunday. A crew member was injured and the incident has triggered a probe by the country's safety regulators. What do we know about the near-miss collision? The Jetstar A320 was taxiing for takeoff to the Gold Coast in the state of Queensland when its flight crew saw the Qatar Airways Boeing 777 — which was being towed by an aircraft tug — in close proximity on a crossing taxiway, the Australian Transport Safety Bureau (ATSB) said in a statement. "Both aircraft were stopped abruptly", the statement said, leading to a Jestar cabin crew member moving through the cabin being injured and the connection between the 777 nose gear and aircraft tug suffering damage. The injured crew member was treated by paramedics. How are Australian authorities handling the incident? The ATSB said that investigators were gathering data from both the planes, air traffic control, and interviewing crew and tug operators to determine the cause of the near collision. The regulator put out a call for witnesses at the airport to send in any visuals of the incident. Jetstar — which is a low-cost subsidiary of Australia's national carrier Qantas — said it was also conducting its own investigation. "Our aircraft was following ⁠instructions ​by Air Traffic Control when the ​pilots were forced to brake firmly after another aircraft came in ​close proximity," a ‌Jetstar spokesperson said. There was no immediate statement from Qatar Airways, which is the flag carrier of Qatar. Meanwhile, flights at Sydney Airport were experiencing delays following the incident, government agency Airservices Australia said. Sunday's incident ⁠comes a day after Sydney Airport witnessed widespread delays ⁠sparked by Airservices Australia authorizing "departure spacing" due to roster issues with air traffic controllers. Composite: Isabella Finholdt/NurPhoto/Shutterstock, Douglas Shineidr/Getty View image in fullscreen Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (left) is seeking a fourth term, with the far-right senator Flávio Bolsonaro standing in his way. Composite: Isabella Finholdt/NurPhoto/Shutterstock, Douglas Shineidr/Getty Brazil Polls close in first round of Brazil’s high-stakes presidential election Leftwing incumbent Lula trying to fight off close rival Flávio Bolsonaro, far-right son of jailed ex-president Tiago Rogero in Rio de Janeiro Sun 4 Oct 2026 09.52 EDT First published on Sun 4 Oct 2026 04.53 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The polls have closed in the first round of Brazil’s highly polarised and high-stakes presidential election that could change not only the direction of Latin America’s largest country but that of the entire region. The election pits the leftwing president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, who is seeking a fourth non-consecutive term, against the far-right senator Flávio Bolsonaro, an ally of Donald Trump and the son of the former president Jair Bolsonaro, who is serving a 27-year sentence for attempting a coup after his failed 2022 re-election attempt. Late on Sunday Bolsonaro was leading Lula in partial results. With results in from almost 65% of the country, Bolsonaro had 49.8% to Lula’s 42.25%, while several other candidates stood in the single digits. Lula and Bolsonaro have alternated as frontrunners in the final stretch, making the outcome unpredictable. In recent days both have focused on persuading undecided voters in hopes of reaching 50% plus one vote; if neither does, there will be a runoff on 25 October. Brazil is one of the few Latin American countries that still has a leftwing government after a wave of rightwing and far-right electoral victories across the region and the US takeover of Venezuela after the capture of Nicolás Maduro. The 80-year-old Lula has positioned himself as one of the last regional leaders still willing to say no to Trump, and has recently accused the US president of trying to interfere in Brazil’s election in Bolsonaro’s favour . View image in fullscreen Lula embraces a child as he leaves a polling station in São Bernardo do Campo after casting his vote on Sunday. Photograph: Alexandre Meneghini/Reuters Like his father, who was Brazil’s president during Trump’s first term, Flávio Bolsonaro, 45, frequently praises the US president and has pledged to join the US-led anti-drug-cartel coalition that has killed dozens of people in airstrikes and carried out military operations across the region. Voting on Sunday morning in São Bernardo do Campo, the industrial city where his political career began nearly half a century ago, Lula said: “People will have to choose between strengthening democracy and barbarism.” The incumbent played down polls released on Saturday that showed the race was wide open – they suggested either candidate could finish ahead and force a runoff, or even win outright on Sunday. “The poll that matters will be carried out today,” he said. View image in fullscreen Flávio Bolsonaro with his wife, Fernanda, after voting in Rio de Janeiro. Photograph: Silvia Izquierdo/AP Flávio Bolsonaro, who voted in Rio de Janeiro’s north zone, urged supporters of other rightwing candidates to switch to him in a “protest vote”. “Our internal polls show people who would have voted for other candidates, who are also against Lula, already voting for Flávio Bolsonaro … I hope it’s enough to give us victory in the first round,” he said. Claudinei Ferreira Viana, 45, a workshop manager in Pinhais in Paraná state, is one of the senator’s supporters. “My first choice would be Jair Bolsonaro but, since he is under house arrest and there is no other rightwing candidate strong enough to take on the current president, I’m going with Flávio,” he said. 3:43 How Trump is meddling in Brazil’s election – explainer At the beginning of the year, polls suggested Bolsonaro voters would have preferred a ticket led by the São Paulo governor, Tarcísio de Freitas, or the former first lady Michelle Bolsonaro. But the former president chose his eldest son. The campaign was also marked by a scandal in which the senator was caught on tape asking a banker accused of corruption for $26.8m (£20m) to fund a film about his father , as well as speculation that Bolsonaro might strip the country’s widely cherished patron saint of her status, but he has nevertheless remained highly competitive. View image in fullscreen Flávio Bolsonaro during an open-top campaign parade through the Campo Grande district of Rio de Janeiro on Saturday. Photograph: Bruna Prado/AP For many analysts, that reflects a combination of a straightforward transfer of his father’s voter base – Jair Bolsonaro lost to Lula by less than two percentage points in 2022 – and an anti-Lula vote, with the president still facing high rejection rates despite strong social and economic indicators . The incumbent’s campaign has also been hit by corruption allegations – still under investigation – involving his son and a former aide, as well as a scandal involving supreme court justices , which, despite having no connection to Lula, is seen as fuelling an “anti-system” vote and by extension an anti-incumbent one. View image in fullscreen Lula parading through São Paulo on Saturday. Photograph: Sebastião Moreira/EPA Brazilians will also elect 27 state governors, members of state legislatures, all 513 federal congress members and 54 of the country’s 81 senators in Sunday’s vote. AMC, 40, who asked to be identified only by her initials because she fears reprisals from the local conservative government where she works in the interior of Amazonas state, will vote for Lula on Sunday “because of the many programmes he created to support the most vulnerable groups”. “Jair Bolsonaro weakened protections for Indigenous peoples, and everything Lula has done over the past four years to strengthen those protections and protect the Amazon would be seriously threatened if his son came to power,” she said. https://www.dw.com/en/estonia-closes-bor.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5PTSN Prefer DW on Google Estonia was one of the few EU states that allowed border crossings to and from Russia Image: Hendrik Osula/AP Photo/picture alliance Advertisement Estonia foiled an attempted Russian arson attack on a drone fractory, authorities said on Sunday, prompting the country to close all border crossings with its larger neighbor. Prime Minister Karsten Michal said that Russia's GRU intelligence service had attempted to sabotage the Estonian defence company Threod Systems in Viimsi on Saturday night. He said "extensive damage" had been averted after a response by law enforcement, who detained the suspected attackers. "This is part of Russia's broader hybrid war against Europe, with the aim of decreasing support to Ukraine and pressure on Russia," Michal said. There was no immediate comment from Russia. Estonia to close border crossings with Russia Hours after the announcement, Estonia's Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna said the country would close all border crossings with Russia by December 1. "Russia must understand that hostile actions against Estonia come with consequences. Attempts to intimidate, destabilise, or undermine our security will not go unanswered," he said on social media. "Closing the border crossings will reduce Russia's ability to conduct hostile activities in Estonia and strengthen our efforts to prevent sanctions circumvention." Estonia has a number of border crossings with Russia, and has until now remained one of the few European Union member states that allowed crossings.
